blocks.text: Every tool a model can call needs a way to describe exactly what input it expects.
That description is called a schema, and it is the contract between the tool and whatever is calling it, human or model.
In this lesson we will pull that schema apart piece by piece, and see how a model uses it, and how a server should check it before trusting it.
1. What a Tool Schema Describes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586020-3194857.png
A tool's schema is a precise, machine readable description of the shape its input must take.
It lists every parameter the tool accepts, what type each one is, which ones are mandatory, and what each one means.
Without a schema, a model would be guessing blindly at what to send, and a server would have no clean way to check what arrived.

blocks.title: Schema is not the same as documentation
blocks.content: A schema is structured and checkable by code. A plain English description in a readme is helpful for people, but a schema is what software actually validates against.

blocks.text: 2. JSON Schema as the Language of Tool Inputs
MCP tools describe their input using JSON Schema, a widely used standard for describing the shape of JSON data.
JSON Schema was not invented for MCP, it already had years of use across APIs, config files, and form generators before tools ever needed it.
That maturity matters, because it means validators, editors, and documentation tools already understand it out of the box.
3. The Anatomy of an inputSchema Object
Almost every tool's inputSchema starts the same way, with type set to object.
Inside that object sit two key fields, properties and required.
properties is a map from parameter name to a small schema describing that one parameter's type and meaning.
required is simply an array of the parameter names that must be present for the call to make sense.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","What it holds"],"rows":[["type","Almost always object, since arguments arrive as a single JSON object"],["properties","One entry per parameter name, each with its own type and description"],["required","An array listing which parameter names cannot be left out"],["additionalProperties","Optional flag to reject any parameter not explicitly declared"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Required vs Optional Parameters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586020-565704500.png
A parameter is required when the tool genuinely cannot do its job without it.
Everything else should be optional, ideally with a sensible default described in plain language.
Marking too many parameters as required makes a tool brittle and annoying to call for simple cases.
Marking too few as required makes a tool fragile, since it may run with missing pieces and produce a confusing result.
Here city and max_price are required, guests is optional and falls back to a default of 1.
5. String Parameters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586020-235586723.png
A string parameter is the simplest and most common type, used for names, free text, identifiers, and short labels.
JSON Schema lets you tighten a string further with things like minLength, maxLength, or a pattern for expected formats.
Adding a pattern like this catches an obviously malformed email before the tool ever tries to use it.
6. Number and Boolean Parameters
Number covers both integers and decimals, while integer is a stricter version that rejects decimals entirely.
Boolean is just true or false, useful for simple on or off style flags such as breakfast_included.

blocks.title: Use minimum and maximum generously
blocks.content: Bounding numeric ranges catches nonsense values early, like a negative price or a guest count of zero, without writing a single line of custom code.

blocks.text: 7. Array Parameters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586021-89164225.png
An array parameter holds a list of values, and its items field describes the type each entry in that list must be.
Arrays are a natural fit for anything a caller might want to supply more than one of, like a list of amenities or a set of tags.
You can also bound how many items are allowed with minItems and maxItems, which is handy for preventing an absurdly long list.
8. Object Parameters and Nesting
A parameter can itself be an object, with its own nested properties and required list.
This is useful when a group of values naturally belongs together, like a date range with a start and an end.
Nesting is powerful, but it is easy to overdo, and a schema nested many levels deep becomes hard for a model to fill correctly.
9. Enum Parameters for Constrained Choices
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586021-972026208.png
An enum restricts a string, or any type really, to one value from a fixed list you provide.
Enums are perfect for anything with a small, known set of valid options, like a sort order or a status.
Using an enum instead of a free text string removes an entire category of typos and made up values before validation even runs.
A quick recap of the six core types

items: string, for text, names, and free form values
number, for anything numeric including decimals
boolean, for a simple true or false flag
array, for a list of values of some declared item type
object, for a group of related nested properties
enum, for a value constrained to a fixed known set of options

blocks.text: 10. How an LLM Reads a Schema to Decide Arguments

blocks.alt: How an LLM Reads a Schema to Decide Arguments
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586021-759257099.png
When a model is deciding whether and how to call a tool, it reads three things together, the tool name, its description, and its inputSchema.
The schema tells the model exactly which fields exist, what type each one must be, and which ones it absolutely must supply.
The model then maps whatever the user actually said onto those fields, choosing sensible values for anything the user left implicit.
A vague or missing description on a parameter makes this mapping step much harder, and a model may guess wrong or skip a field entirely.
11. From Model Output to a Concrete Tool Call
Once the model has decided what to fill in, it emits a structured arguments object matching the schema's shape as closely as it can.
That object then travels from the model, through whatever client is orchestrating the conversation, to the actual tool implementation.
Notice how the model can still get a field wrong, sending max_price as a string instead of a number, which is exactly why validation on the server side still matters.
12. Validating Incoming Arguments Before Running a Tool

blocks.alt: Validating Incoming Arguments Before Running a Tool
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586529-86735985.png
A server should never simply trust that arguments arriving from a model already match the schema.
Before running any tool logic, the arguments object should be checked field by field against the declared inputSchema.
This single habit, validate first and run second, prevents an enormous class of bugs and confusing failures downstream.
The jsonschema library here does the heavy lifting, checking types, required fields, enums, and bounds all in one call.
13. What Good Validation Rejects
A solid validation step catches several distinct kinds of problems, not just a single missing field.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Problem","Example","What validation should do"],"rows":[["Missing required field","max_price left out entirely","Reject with a message naming the missing field"],["Wrong type","max_price sent as the string 5000","Reject with a message naming the expected type"],["Value out of range","guests sent as 0 when minimum is 1","Reject with a message naming the bound that was violated"],["Value outside an enum","sort_by sent as popularity","Reject and list the allowed values"],["Unexpected extra field","A field not declared anywhere in properties","Reject if additionalProperties is set to false"]]}

blocks.title: Fail loudly, not quietly
blocks.content: A tool that silently ignores a bad value and runs anyway produces a result that looks fine but is actually wrong. A clear rejection is far more useful than a wrong answer.

blocks.text: 14. Writing Clear Parameter Descriptions
The description field on each parameter is not decoration, it is the main thing a model reads to decide what value to put there.
A good description states what the value represents, gives a short concrete example, and mentions any default if the parameter is optional.

items: State what the value represents in plain words, not just repeating the field name
Include a short example value, especially for formats like dates or currencies
Mention the default explicitly for any optional parameter
Note units when a number could be ambiguous, such as rupees versus dollars or minutes versus hours
Keep it short, one clear sentence beats three vague ones

blocks.text: 15. Common Schema Design Patterns
A few small habits make schemas noticeably easier for both models and humans to work with.
Keep required lists short, group related optional fields into one nested object when it makes sense, and always set additionalProperties to false on tools handling sensitive actions.
Worked Example
Let us walk through the search_hotels tool end to end, from schema to a rejected call to a fixed call.
A user asks to find a hotel in Goa under five thousand rupees, and the model produces this call.
Validation fails here, because max_price arrived as the string 5000 instead of a number.

code.content: { "error": "Invalid arguments: '5000' is not of type 'number' at max_price" }

blocks.text: Once the model, or the client layer, corrects the type, the same call passes cleanly and the tool runs.
Common Mistakes

items: Marking almost every parameter as required, so simple calls become needlessly hard to make
Leaving descriptions blank or just repeating the parameter name, giving the model nothing to work with
Using a plain string when an enum would remove an entire category of invalid values
Skipping server side validation because the model is assumed to always send correct types
Never stating a default for optional parameters, forcing users and models to guess
Nesting objects many levels deep when a flatter shape would be far easier to fill correctly

blocks.text: Practice
Design an inputSchema for a tool called book_flight that needs origin, destination, and departure_date as required strings, and an optional seat_class limited to economy, business, or first.
Then write the JavaScript validation error you would expect if seat_class arrives as luxury.
Key Takeaway
A tool's schema is the single source of truth for what it expects, and both the model and the server should treat it that way.
The model leans on clear types, enums, and descriptions to decide what to send, while the server leans on the same schema to validate what actually arrived before ever running the tool.
